title: Choosing to Rise: My Journey Beyond the Tumor
journey:
I still remember the day my life split into two parts — *before* and *after*. Before, I was just Rajan Menon, a regular 24-year-old chasing deadlines, arguing with my mother about eating on time, and dreaming about a future I thought I had complete control over. After… I became a patient.

It started with headaches. Not the usual kind you ignore with a cup of tea or a quick nap — these were sharp, blinding pains that felt like something inside my skull was trying to claw its way out. I brushed it off for weeks. Stress, I told myself. Too much screen time. Too little sleep.

Until one morning, I collapsed.

When I woke up in the hospital, my parents were standing there — silent, pale, and broken in a way I had never seen before. That’s when the doctor said it: “You have a brain tumor.”

Everything went numb.

I didn’t cry immediately. I didn’t react at all. It felt like I was watching someone else’s life fall apart. But that night, when the hospital lights dimmed and the machines beeped steadily beside me, reality hit. I was terrified. Not of pain — but of disappearing. Of becoming a memory too soon.

The days that followed were a blur of tests, scans, and medical terms I didn’t understand. Surgery was the only option. Risky, they said. There were chances I might not wake up. Or worse — wake up not being *me* anymore.

The night before surgery, I wrote letters. To my parents. To my best friend. Even to myself. I didn’t want to leave without saying everything I had kept inside.

But somewhere between fear and acceptance, something changed. I decided — if I was going to fight, I would fight with everything I had.

The surgery lasted 8 hours.

I don’t remember much, just fragments — voices, lights, and then darkness. When I finally woke up, I couldn’t move properly. My body felt чужд (strange), like it didn’t belong to me. Speaking was difficult. Walking was worse. But I was alive.

And that… that was enough to begin again.

Recovery was harder than I ever imagined. People think survival ends with surgery — it doesn’t. That’s where the real battle begins. Learning to speak clearly, to walk steadily, to remember simple things — it felt like rebuilding myself piece by piece.

There were days I wanted to give up. Days when frustration turned into anger, and anger into silence. But my parents never left my side. My mother would sit beside me for hours, holding my hand like I was a child again. My father, who rarely showed emotions, cried when he thought I wasn’t looking.

Slowly, painfully, I improved.

Months later, I walked out of the hospital — not as the same Rajan Menon, but as someone stronger, someone who had stared at the edge and stepped back.

Today, I still carry scars. Some visible, some not. I still have moments of fear. But I also have something I never had before — gratitude.

Life isn’t something I take for granted anymore.

Because when you’ve come that close to losing everything, even the smallest things — a sunrise, a laugh, a quiet moment with family — feel like miracles.

And I am living proof that even when life breaks you… you can still choose to rise. ❤️
medications: Surgery (8 hours), Physical Therapy, Speech Therapy, and unwavering family support.
author: Rajan Menon
